Hi Alex / Samira 

Quick technical answers and a recommended starting config that should meet your p95/p99 targets while controlling cost. TL;DR: configure a small warm pool + fast horizontal scale with short ramp concurrency; tune queueing to avoid head-of-line blocking. Details below.

1) Latency targets and configuration assumptions- Baseline model latency (single-request, streaming): 80-120ms median on our optimized CPU/GPU backends depending on model family.- To achieve p95 <= 300ms during steady-state at ~120 TPS: we recommend a minimum pool capacity that supports ~150 concurrent in-flight token-generation contexts (buffer for spikes).

2) Warm pool sizing (recommended starter)- Warm pool concept: pre-warmed worker slots with loaded model and primed KV-cache so they can start serving streaming requests with minimal per-request overhead.- Recommended: warm_pool_min = 8 workers, warm_pool_buffer = +25% => start with 10 warm workers for your baseline. Each worker handles ~12 concurrent streaming contexts comfortably (depends on model and instance type), so 10 workers ~= 120 concurrent contexts.

3) Burst scaling / scale-up times- Hot scale-up (using warm pool): adding capacity from warm_pool happens in ~2-6s (placement + connection), assuming available warm slots.- Cold scale-up (spinning new instances & model load): typical cold start 60-90s for GPU-backed instances (model load + JIT/kernels), 30-45s for optimized CPU instances with quantized models.
- For your 45s bursts: rely on warm pool + short buffer autoscale policy rather than cold starts. If bursts exceed warm pool, the autoscaler will queue requests briefly while new capacity comes up  we recommend avoiding that by setting warm_pool_padding to accommodate the 800 TPS peak for the 30-45s window.

4) Queueing behavior and SLO enforcement- Our runtime uses per-route request queues with prioritized routing: UI/low-latency routes can be configured to preempt batch/low-priority work.- Recommended queue policy: bounded queue with rejection at 200ms wait (FIR) for latency-sensitive routes; fallback to smaller model variant if queueing would breach SLO.

5) Concurrency & batching tradeoffs- Concurrency per worker increases throughput but can increase p99 latency if token-generation contends for GPU memory/bandwidth. For streaming workloads, we bias toward lower concurrency with aggressive continuous batching to keep p95 low.

6) Operational knobs we suggest you test in PoC- warm_pool_min = 10- warm_pool_max = 30 (allow autoscaler headroom for sustained growth)- scale_up_step = +5 workers / 3s (aggressive for bursty patterns)- queue_threshold_ms = 200 (reject or fallback)- fallback_model = smaller-quantized variant for tail degradation

7) Cost/latency trade estimate (very rough)- Baseline with 10 warm workers: expected steady-state p95 < 250ms, handle ~120 TPS with headroom.
- To safely absorb 800 TPS bursts without rejecting: warm_pool ~28-32 workers depending on instance type  this obviously increases cost. A pragmatic approach: keep a moderate warm pool (10-12) + short pre-warming policy triggered on predictable EOD signals to ramp to 30 workers 60s before batch window.

I'll bring a short simulation of these numbers to Tues's call so we can adjust to your instance preferences and budget.
